demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
He is 62, a European man who has spent most of his adult life behind the counter of a neighborhood bank, the kind of teller customers know by name. He is careful with numbers, steady with routines, and proud of being the person who does not make mistakes. Before the accident, he describes himself as patient and dependable, someone who double-checks locks, balances his drawer to the cent, and drives the same route home every day. He is married, and he and his wife have settled into a quiet life built around work, errands, and visits with family on weekends.

The event happens on an ordinary weekday evening at the end of autumn. He leaves the bank later than usual after helping close out a discrepancy in the accounts. It is already getting dark, and a light rain has started. He is tired, thinking about dinner and replaying the day’s transactions in his head. At an intersection not far from home, he turns left. He does not see the cyclist until the last second. He remembers a flash of reflective fabric, the thud against the front of the car, and then a silence that feels impossible. When he gets out, the bicycle is twisted on the road and the rider is on the ground, moving but clearly badly hurt. He calls emergency services with shaking hands and keeps saying, “I didn’t see him, I didn’t see him,” as if repeating it might undo what has happened.

The cyclist survives but sustains serious injuries. In the weeks afterward, everyone around him tells him it was an accident. The police investigation does not find recklessness or intoxication. Even so, he feels something inside him harden into certainty: a decent man would have seen him. He cannot stop picturing the moment of impact. The image breaks into his mind while he is brushing his teeth, while he is counting cash, while he is standing at the kitchen sink. At night he jolts awake with his heart racing, hearing again the sound of the collision. Sometimes in the dream he is frozen behind the wheel; sometimes he is the one lying in the street while strangers stare.

He returns to work because he believes he should. At the bank he keeps his voice calm and polite, but the rhythm that used to comfort him is gone. When a customer drops a coin tray or a drawer slams unexpectedly, his whole body jerks. He becomes distracted in the middle of transactions and has to recount money two and three times. He worries that he will make a serious error, that one lapse will prove he is no longer trustworthy. He used to chat easily with customers, especially older regulars. Now he avoids eye contact if they mention cycling, rain, traffic, or accidents in the news. A child once runs past the line wearing a bright safety jacket, and for a moment he cannot breathe.

Driving becomes the center of his life in a way he never would have imagined. He starts taking long detours to avoid the intersection. Then he begins asking his wife to drive whenever they go anywhere together. If he must drive alone to work, he grips the wheel so tightly his hands ache. He slows excessively before turns and scans the sidewalks over and over, certain that someone is about to appear in front of him. Cars behind him honk, which leaves him sweating and ashamed. More than once he parks a few streets away from the bank because he cannot bring himself to complete the final turn near where the accident happened.

At home, his wife notices he is no longer really present. He sits in his chair staring at the television without following the program. He startles when she enters the room unexpectedly. He sleeps in short stretches and often gets up before dawn to check the weather and traffic reports, as if vigilance can prevent some future harm. He has become quieter with family, partly because he does not want to talk about the accident and partly because he believes he has forfeited the right to enjoy himself. When relatives suggest a holiday or a celebratory dinner, he finds reasons not to go. He tells himself he is tired, but underneath is the thought that he should not be out laughing while another man lives with injuries he caused.

The guilt has a moral weight that colors everything. He follows updates about road accidents compulsively, reading each article as if searching for punishment. He wonders about the cyclist’s body, whether he still has pain getting out of bed, whether his family sees him differently now. He imagines meeting him and being unable to speak. At times he catches himself thinking that his whole life can be divided into before that turn and after it. The man who once believed that caution kept people safe now feels frightened by how quickly ordinary life can become irreversible. Even in moments when nothing is happening—standing at his station under fluorescent lights, counting notes into neat stacks—he feels the memory waiting just behind him, ready to break through.
